title: Circuit symbols and circuit diagrams

learning_outcomes.text: recall and use the circuit symbols shown in section 6 of this syllabus
draw and interpret circuit diagrams containing the circuit symbols shown in section 6 of this syllabus

external_knowledge: Topic 9: electric current is measured by an ammeter.
Topic 9: potential difference across a component is measured by a voltmeter.
Topic 9: current, potential difference, resistance and I-V relationships have already been studied.

prior_knowledge_summary: Completed Topic 9 Electricity foundations: current, potential difference, resistance and I-V relationships.
This lesson uses only the measurement roles of current and potential difference. It does not extend their quantitative treatment.
new_learning: Recognise prescribed circuit components from their symbols.
Read connections by tracing wires, junctions and branches rather than by the physical position of symbols on the page.
Translate a written component-and-connection description into a complete circuit diagram.
Place an ammeter in the path whose current is measured and a voltmeter across the two terminals of the component whose potential difference is measured.
not_yet_taught: energy definitions of e.m.f. and potential difference
internal resistance and terminal potential difference

blocks.heading: Three drawings, one electrical circuit
content: A cell, lamp and switch are joined in one loop. Three students sketch the loop in three different shapes: a rectangle, a wide oval and a narrow zigzag. Which drawing represents the real circuit?
All three can be correct. A circuit diagram records components and connections, not the physical shape of the wires on the bench. Predict what must stay unchanged when the drawing is rearranged.

figure.purpose: Create the need to separate circuit connectivity from page layout.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch showing the same cell, open switch and lamp connected in one loop in three visibly different layouts. Use a small colour key to match each component across layouts. Do not label any layout correct or incorrect.
figure.alt_text: Three differently shaped diagrams contain the same cell, switch and lamp in one continuous loop.

blocks.heading: Symbols are a shared circuit language
content: A circuit symbol replaces the appearance of a real component with a simple agreed mark. The mark lets anyone read the circuit without needing a photograph of the equipment.

Learn each symbol by its distinguishing feature. A cell has one long line and one short line. A battery repeats that pair. A fixed resistor is a plain rectangle. A variable resistor adds a diagonal arrow. A thermistor adds a diagonal temperature marker. An LDR places a resistor inside a circle with arrows pointing towards it.

Meters are circles carrying a letter. A is an ammeter, V is a voltmeter and G is a galvanometer. A lamp is a circle with a cross. A diode uses a triangle-free diode mark, while an LED adds arrows pointing away to show emitted light.

figure.purpose: Build accurate visual recall by grouping prescribed symbols through their distinguishing features.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper symbol family chart with neat hand-drawn symbols for cell, battery, switch, lamp, fixed resistor, variable resistor, thermistor, LDR, diode, LED, ammeter, voltmeter and galvanometer. Group related symbols with restrained colours. Keep labels short and avoid circuit-law equations.
figure.alt_text: A grouped chart shows prescribed source, resistor, sensor, diode, lamp, switch and meter symbols.

blocks.heading: Read wires as paths and junctions
content: Begin at one point and trace every continuous wire. If the path returns to its starting point without a gap, it is a complete loop. A switch drawn open makes a gap; a switch drawn closed completes the connection.

A filled junction dot shows that wires meet electrically. Crossing lines without a junction dot do not automatically form a connection. A branch begins where one path divides and ends where the paths meet again.

Two components may look side by side on the page yet lie on different branches. Another pair may be far apart on the page but belong to the same uninterrupted path. Connectivity decides the circuit, not distance or drawing direction.

figure.purpose: Teach complete paths, breaks, junctions and branches as connectivity features.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison panel with four small traces: complete loop, open-switch gap, true junction with dot, and crossing wires without a junction. Use coloured path tracing and sparse callouts.
figure.alt_text: Four sketches compare a complete loop, an open gap, connected wires at a junction and crossing wires that are not joined.

blocks.heading: Turn a written description into a diagram
content: Suppose a cell, closed switch, ammeter and lamp must form one complete path, and a voltmeter must measure the potential difference across the lamp.
First draw the main loop. Place the cell, switch, ammeter and lamp on that one continuous path. The order around a simple loop can change without changing which components share the path.
Next find the two terminals of the lamp. Draw a separate branch from one lamp terminal, through the voltmeter, to the other lamp terminal. The voltmeter is now across the lamp only.

Finally trace the diagram. The main loop has no gap, the ammeter lies in the measured current path, and the voltmeter branch touches both ends of the lamp. This connection check is independent of how tidy the page looks.

figure.purpose: Model a complete description-to-schematic construction and an independent connectivity check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper four-step worked layout: component list, main loop, voltmeter branch added across lamp, and coloured trace check. Use original arrangement and standard symbols. No numerical values or circuit-law equations.
figure.alt_text: A four-step layout builds a circuit with a cell, switch, ammeter and lamp in the main loop and a voltmeter across the lamp.

blocks.heading: Meters follow the quantity being measured
content: From Topic 9, an ammeter measures current. To measure the current in a path, charge must pass through the ammeter as it follows that path, so the ammeter belongs in that path.

A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points. To measure across one component, its two leads connect to the two terminals of that component, so it sits on a separate branch across the component.

Think of the ammeter as a gate on a route and the voltmeter as a bridge between two endpoints. The words in path and across two terminals are more reliable than memorising where the meter appeared in one drawing.

figure.purpose: Give a second causal explanation for series ammeter and parallel voltmeter placement.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper split comparison. Left traces one coloured current path through an ammeter. Right highlights the two terminals of a lamp and the voltmeter branch joining them. Include the phrases 'in the path' and 'across two terminals'.
figure.alt_text: An ammeter lies in a highlighted current path, while a voltmeter connects across the two terminals of a lamp.

blocks.heading: A neat-looking diagram can still be wrong
content: It feels natural to trust a symmetric diagram or to call every pair of nearby components parallel. That visual shortcut fails because page position does not determine electrical connection.

Trace the wires instead. Components are on the same path only when the wire carries you through one and then the other without a branching choice. A component is across another only when its two ends join the same two junctions.
A second common error is to place both meters in the main loop. That may look tidy, but it does not put the voltmeter across the selected component. Always check its two endpoints.

figure.purpose: Repair layout-based reasoning and the common all-meters-in-one-loop error.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper error-correction panel. Show one tidy but wrongly connected meter circuit and one visually irregular but correctly connected equivalent. Overlay endpoint dots and path tracing, with a small correction arrow but no answer to any practice item.
figure.alt_text: A tidy circuit with a misplaced voltmeter is contrasted with a less symmetric circuit whose meter connections are correct.

blocks.heading: A four-check circuit routine
content: Check 1: use the prescribed symbol for every named component. Check 2: trace each intended loop and find any gap. Check 3: mark every true junction and identify each branch. Check 4: test meter endpoints: an ammeter lies in the measured path and a voltmeter joins both ends of the measured component.
Redrawing bent or stretched wires does not change the circuit if every component keeps the same connections. Adding or removing a junction, branch or gap does change it.

This lesson stops at symbols and connectivity. The next lessons will attach energy meaning to e.m.f. and potential difference, then analyse internal resistance. Do not use those later ideas to solve this lesson's practice.

concepts_taught: complete loops, gaps, junctions and branches
misconceptions_addressed: Nearby or symmetric components must share the same electrical connection.
Every crossing of drawn wires is a junction.
Both ammeter and voltmeter belong in the main loop.

Complete loops, branches and junctions can be traced from a circuit diagram.
An ammeter is placed in the measured current path and a voltmeter across the selected component.
